title: Dedicated capacity: capacity surge & degraded throughput playbook
author: Jordan Alvarez
body:
SUMMARY
--------
This playbook describes the customer-facing and internal runbook for handling capacity surges and degraded throughput for Redwood Dedicated and Private deployments. It covers detection, immediate mitigation, coordinated scaling, fallback routing, communications, and post-incident follow-up. Use this when a customer reports sustained throughput degradation, elevated queueing/backpressure, or when platform telemetry shows p95 token latency or request-level latency exceeding SLOs for >5 minutes.

SCOPE & APPLICABILITY
---------------------
- Applies to: Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools) and Private (VPC / on-prem) deployments.
- Not covered: Hosted API transient slowdowns caused by public network issues (use platform incident channel).
- Typical customers: enterprise customers with provisioned capacity or autoscale policies.

IMPACT CLASSIFICATION (Triage categories)
-----------------------------------------
- Sev-1 (Critical): Customer-facing production impact, >20% of requests failing or latency >5× p95, customer is in a live critical workflow (billing, safety-critical). Immediate paging.
- Sev-2 (High): Sustained throughput drop causing degraded UX for a subset of endpoints (>10% error or 2× p95 latency), mitigations required within 30–60 minutes.
- Sev-3 (Medium): Intermittent slowdowns, sporadic queuing, or degraded batch job throughput. Monitor and resolve during working hours.

DETECTION & KEY SIGNALS
----------------------
- Automatic alarms (preferred):
  - Per-route p95 latency > 2× SLO for 5 consecutive minutes.
  - Queue depth (service-side request backlog) > configured threshold (default 100 requests).
  - GPU utilization >95% sustained for 3 minutes AND tail latency spike.
  - Autoscaler thrashing: frequent scale events with no restored throughput.
- Customer report: high-latency or timeouts reported by a customer success contact or PagerDuty.

IMMEDIATE MITIGATION (first 0–15 minutes)
------------------------------------------
1) Acknowledge and set status: open incident in Jira/Incident Manager, set preliminary priority using classification above.
2) Notify channels: post to Slack #support-dedicated and tag @oncall-sre and the CSM assigned to the account. Use incident header: [DEDICATED-SURGE] <customer-name> — <severe|high|medium>.
3) Run fast health checks (commands):
   - Check per-node GPU and host metrics: `kubectl -n redwood get pods -l app=runtime -o wide` and `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory --format=csv` (for on-prem/Private runbooks use provided admin access).
   - Check autoscaler state: `kubectl -n redwood get hpa,scaledobject -o yaml` and platform autoscaler dashboard.
   - Check request queues and backlog: query metrics `service_queue_length{customer=\"<id>\"}` and `request_latency_seconds_bucket`.
4) Short-term capacity relief: if allowed by contract, trigger burst pool grow or enable burst policy documented in the customer's Dedicated settings. If no burst available, proceed to fallback routing (see below).

TRIAGE & DIAGNOSTICS (15–45 minutes)
-----------------------------------
Follow these parallel investigations. Assign leads for: Metrics, Runtime, Networking, Customer comms.
- Metrics lead (SRE):
  - Confirm which routes/models are impacted (per-route dashboards).
  - Check model variant: heavy quantization or long-context variant? Confirm sequence length distribution spike.
  - Validate whether prefix cache (KV cache) hit rate dropped: `kv_cache_hit_rate{customer=\"<id>\"}`.
- Runtime lead (serving runtime engineer):
  - Check batching behavior: are requests being continuously merged into large batches causing queuing? Review batch size histograms.
  - Inspect logs for OOMs, kernel failures, CUDA timeouts.
  - Validate kernel selection anomalies (e.g., fallback to slower kernels).
- Networking lead (infra):
  - Verify egress/ingress network error rates, firewall logs for Private.
  - For Dedicated, validate intra-pod networking and NLB health checks.
- Customer success lead (CSM):
  - Start proactive comms: confirm scope, affected endpoints, recommended temporary mitigations customer can apply (e.g., reduce client concurrency, reduce max tokens).

MITIGATION OPTIONS (ordered by speed and impact)
------------------------------------------------
1) Toggle client-level soft-limits: advise customer to reduce client concurrency by 30–50% and reduce requested max_tokens for immediate relief.
2) Enable/expand burst pool: if the customer has burst capacity, authorize and scale it up.
3) Autoscaler tuning: temporarily increase max replicas or GPU instance type if policy allows.
4) Fallback to smaller model variant: route traffic to a compatible, lower-latency model (e.g., 8-bit quantized variant) with customer approval for quality tradeoff.
5) Route non-critical traffic to hosted fallback: for hybrid customers, shift lower-priority jobs to Redwood Hosted for duration of incident.
6) Live patch (runtime): if a known kernel regression is found, apply hotfix per runtime release playbook.
7) Full capacity rotate: drain and replace nodes exhibiting stuck processes. Use with caution and during low-traffic windows when possible.

ESCALATION MATRIX & CONTACTS
---------------------------
- Customer Success Lead (primary): <CSM name> — primary contact for customer comms.
- SRE on-call: platform PagerDuty — handles infrastructure and scaling.
- Runtime Engineering: @runtime-team Slack handle, escalation to runtime lead if root is serving-level.
- Product Ops: for contractual approvals to enable burst/reserved capacity.
- Exec escalation: for prolonged Sev-1 (>2 hours) notify Director of Customer Success and Head of SRE.

Use this escalation template in Slack and email (replace tokens):
- Slack header: `[DEDICATED-SURGE] <customer> — <sev>`
- Short message: `Impact: <routes>/<percentage>. Observed: p95 latency <value> (SLO <value>). Actions taken: <list>. Next steps: <list>. Owners: @sre_oncall, @runtime_lead, @<CSM>.`

COMMUNICATIONS (Customer-facing)
--------------------------------
- Initial acknowledgement (within 15 minutes):
  - Subject: Redwood Incident notice — Elevated latency for <customer> dedicated deployment
  - Body (short): `We are investigating increased latency on your dedicated deployment. Our SRE and Runtime teams are actively triaging. Recommended temporary mitigation: reduce client concurrency by 30% and reduce max_tokens where possible. We'll provide an update within 30 minutes.`
- Status updates: every 30 minutes for Sev-1, every 60 minutes for Sev-2. Include: root cause hypothesis, mitigations executed, ETA for next update.
- Resolution note: include steps taken, customer impact summary (times, percent of requests affected), and recommended post-incident actions for the customer.

ROLLBACK OR DEGRADATION STRATEGIES
----------------------------------
- If a runtime hotfix increases risk, prefer route-level fallback to a previous model variant instead of a runtime patch during active high load.
- If scaling triggers cascading failures, revert to last-known-good autoscale configuration and then apply smaller increments.

POST-INCIDENT REVIEW & ACTIONS
-----------------------------
1) Within 48 hours: create an incident report with timeline, metrics snapshots, decisions, and customer communications. Owner: incident commander (IC).
2) Within 7 days: perform RCA with SRE, Runtime, CS, and Product. Determine corrective actions, owners, and ETA.
3) Action examples:
   - Adjust default autoscaler thresholds for similar workloads.
   - Add additional burst-pool quotas for customers with predictable traffic spikes.
   - Update onboarding docs to include recommended client-side concurrency controls.
4) Postmortem sharing: redact sensitive items and share with customer (if requested) and internal stakeholders.

RUNBOOK OWNER & REVIEW CADENCE
-----------------------------
- Owner: Customer Success (playbook custodian) and SRE (technical custodian).
- Quarterly review or after any Sev-1 incident related to capacity.

APPENDIX: QUICK CHECKLIST & COMMANDS
-----------------------------------
Quick checklist (first 15 minutes):
- [ ] Open incident ticket and set priority.
- [ ] Notify Slack channels and tag on-call and CSM.
- [ ] Run `kubectl` / `nvidia-smi` checks and capture top 3 anomalies.
- [ ] Query queue depth and p95 latency for impacted routes.
- [ ] Ask customer to reduce concurrency and max_tokens.

Useful commands and metrics: (replace <customer-id> and <namespace>)
- `kubectl -n <namespace> get pods -l customer=<customer-id> -o wide`
- `kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> --tail 200`
- `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,temperature.gpu --format=csv`
- Metrics queries: `sum(rate(requests_total{customer=\"<id>\"}[1m])) by (route)`, `histogram_quantile(0.95, sum(rate(request_latency_seconds_bucket{customer=\"<id>\"}[5m])) by (le))`

CONFIG TABLE (common thresholds used in playbook)
------------------------------------------------
| Item | Default threshold | Action if exceeded |
| p95 latency (route) | 2× declared route SLO | Trigger triage and notify SRE |
| Queue depth | 100 requests | Apply short-term throttling and review batching |
| GPU utilization | 95% sustained 3m | Check batching and hot loops; consider burst |
| Autoscaler thrash | >6 scale events / 15m | Pause autoscaler or increase stabilization window |

PRIVACY & CUSTOMER CONTRACT NOTES
---------------------------------
- Any scaling > contracted reserved capacity requires Product Ops approval and documented change in contract records.
- For Private/on-prem customers, follow local change-control and maintenance windows unless otherwise permitted by contract.

DOCUMENT HISTORY
----------------
- Created: 2025-09-15 by Jordan Alvarez
- Reviews: Priya Raman, Ethan Brooks, Sofia Chen (2026-02-20)
- Last updated: 2026-02-25 — clarified fallback routing and added autoscaler thrash guidance.
